utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I mention at the outset that the -- in setting out the schedules for Friday, Friday's sittings, the Chamber's order of two days ago inadvertently failed to mention that Friday, the 8th, that is two days' time, we will not be sitting. We will not be sitting on Friday, the 8th. I see Mr. Tapuskovic has no objection to that. And it's Mr. Waespi, who was -- Mr. Sachdeva? Oh, we are still in examination-in-chief, so it's Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Thank you very much for this, but I first have to say something. According to the initial schedule, Witness Vaso Elez was supposed to be examined first and then we changed it to T 53, but now we've had to revert to the initial schedule, so that we will first be examining Witness Vaso Elez. We've notified the Prosecution and they are not opposed to us reverting to the initial schedule, so I'm just notifying Your Honours about this change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Waespi, am I wrong? Did I say something that is not correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, you will recall that we stopped yesterday with a map that was on our screens. Could we please have it back on our screens? Could we enlarge it a little bit more? Now I would like you to go back to this largest space. You explained what it is. And if you can put a large letter S somewhere in the middle of this area?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: This area, the largest area?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the largest area.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The smaller one, could you please mark it with D?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the smallest one, who lived here? Could you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the majority Serb population, the Serb who is had lived there for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with S2?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Last time we got as far as the first incident and the second incident at the Bozic gas station. That's what you were telling us about. And what happened after that, if we can cut a long story short, how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Sachdeva is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm terribly sorry, I understand my learned friend asked for the letter D to be put into the second circle and the letter E is there. I just want to ask what the letter E stands for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: D?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh. Now I wondered whether E stood for D.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it doesn't really matter. We can use letter E or any other letter because the witness has already explained that this is an area where people who had moved there in 1974 moved there. These were people who were moved out of Serbia at that time. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So we understand what the letter E means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, if you're able, can you please tell us when did the people in this area first started arming themselves, in this period that we were talking about? And what kind of weapons did they get?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've already explained, after those incidents, we got organised in our village and we set up village guards. We had hunting rifles. There were quite a few huntsmen in our village. We organised five or six groups, armed with hunting rifles, who controlled this territory along this edge here, this boundary, lest any extremists should break into our territory and cause similar problems as they had in those two or three incidents that we spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what about this area marked with E?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: At night, when we patrolled, those were our neighbours. We would meet them and they also patrolled, and in conversation, we learned that they had also set up a similar system, lest their own extremists in their own ranks should make any other such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any conflicts at that time? What month are we talking about in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was March and early April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges what happened then, after the first few days in April?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after that, somebody notified us, I don't know who that was, but all the villagers of military age went to the Rajlovac barracks. This was the barracks where our assembly point was. Some drills used to be carried out there. And we went there and our Muslim neighbours from the E area, all of us were issued weapons at the Rajlovac barracks on the same day. There were about 200 of us. We were issued 200 weapons, rifles, and they, from Sokolje there were 800 of them and they were issued with 800 rifles and we all went back to our respective villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened then in the period that followed?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that there was a lull up until the 5th of May, when, as we were to learn later, some extremists that were infiltrated into this E area attacked on the 5th of May using all weapons they had, the Rajlovac area. They concentrated their attack on the Rajlovac area. But they also attacked the outskirts of our village, in particular I mean my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please mark the location of the Rajlovac barracks here on this map?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. This is the Rajlovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark it with R, letter R?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then? I apologise, Your Honours. I've already marked the location where the witness used to work with letter R so could we please mark it with K so if we could erase this R?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell the Judges what happened then?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 5th of May, here where my house is, in Bjelice, Boro Bjelica was killed there. This is the first casualty in our municipality. More than 30 shells landed around my house. I managed to evacuate my wife, my two children, my father and my mother, and we moved deeper into our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you move your wife, your father, mother and your two children at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, we moved -- I moved my mother, my father, my two children and all the children in our village across the River Bosna.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to repeat his answer? The interpreters didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Would you repeat your answer, please? The interpreter didn't hear. The answer to the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Just the location where the people were moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Judges where you moved everybody?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife, my two children, my mother, my father, so that would be my family, and all the other inhabitants of our village who were in those categories, children, women, the infirm, they were all moved halfway there to the village of Nelise [phoen] across the River Bosna, to the river -- to the village of Rjecica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us how far did you move?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and other men of military age moved and set up our defence line halfway down the village. I can mark it if you want me to. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And did you hear about the events to the east of these areas that you just marked?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only did we hear about it, we had this terrible experience, maybe some 10 days later, around the 15th of May, maybe 20th of May, in mid-May in other words, from Pofalici a part of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So could you please tell us where from and could you please mark this area and could you please mark this location that you are going to -- that you're going to mark, and if you can pull the letter that I'm going to tell you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is Pofalici. It's a fairly large part of town. That would be about it. [Marks]. This was the majority Serb population there in 90 per cent of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark this area, this circle, with the letter P?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in that area in this period that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Green Beret or the Patriotic League attacked this whole area of Pofalici in those days. They killed more than 100 people. Entire families were wiped out. And the whole population, 5.000 people, moved across Zuc, Debelo Brdo, Perivoj to Rajlovac. If you need me to do so, I can mark their route with an arrow, 5.000 people, including women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please do so, what you just said? Could you just mark this arrow?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, which year is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you can ask the witness. I wouldn't like to offer this information myself. He can give you the exact month and year. So let us hear it from the witness when this happened, when these 5.000 people moved and when 100 people were killed. Let us hear from the witness when this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sure. I just want to say that I normally try to respect the integrity of the counsels by putting my questions to the witness through the counsel as long as the counsel is either in examination-in-chief or cross-examination. It's only when the counsels have finished their examinations and the judges can pose questions directly to the witness that I do so. But, Mr. Witness, can you just tell us which year this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This happened in May of 1992. To be more precise, on the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what happened with these 5.000 people when they arrived at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: These 5.000 people, that is to say 1.000 indigenous people from the area marked S2, crossed over to the barracks and all of them were received at the barracks. They had enough space to provide accommodation for these people for the period of five to 10 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we can just go through this quickly, you showed the line that you reached after the initial conflict and you drew this line. How long did you stay at this separation line vis-a-vis the opposite side and were there any shifts in the ensuing period?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it briefly, the war -- the real war started on that day. As far as the line is concerned, since the army of Republika Srpska was formed very soon thereafter, we established a defence line there. The line was shifted only in one part, that is in the section where we withdrew on the 12th of June 1993 and it was moved a little bit deeper into our territory and that is how it remained until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you draw this in the map? Where is that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: So our line of defence ran from the Miljacka along the railway tracks to the Rajlovac barracks, then it went on through my village of Zabrdje towards Mijatovic Kosa. Then on the other side of the Vis hill, Golo Brdo hill, on the other side of Zuc and all the way to Kobilja Glava. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did this situation remain in place?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 12th of June 1993 until the Dayton Accords were signed, this line did not change.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you put a letter D at the very end of this line?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. I'll put a D at the beginning and at the end as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this line, with respect to the deployment areas of the opposite side, geographically speaking, where was it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us start from Miljacka, from the Miljacka river. This is elevation 490 something. This is the Rajlovac Polje. The line ran along the railway tracks and that is where our positions were. Opposite us was Brijesko Brdo hill, 100 metres high, and the BH army positions were on the hill. So we were in the field and they were on the hill. If we proceed then to more urban area of the neighbourhood, the line goes on to Zuc and Orlic and it stretched or rather ran through a forested area starting from the Mijatovic Kosa, to Vis hill which is around 700 metres, then Golo Brdo elevation, 870, then Zuc 756 and Orlic and all the way to Hum which is the highest hill because there is a TV repeater. The BH television repeater was there. The entire line faced downwards while the entire line of the BH army was on the hills facing downwards towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we save the map with all the markings as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Tapuskovic, I didn't understand what the witness was telling us when he said that both sides had the front line facing downwards. Maybe you would ask him to clarify. It's in the last line, I don't know if you read English. I know that you don't. But in the English version, it came out as the witness was saying that the entire line faced downwards while the entire line of the BH army was on the hills facing downwards towards us. So who was on the top and who was in the bottom? That is unclear according to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, if that is what the transcript says in English, then it's a misinterpretation. I understood the witness in B/C/S very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, witness, can you please explain simply who was on the hills and who was down there in the plain?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire line, to be precise and accurate, the entire defence line of the Rajlovac Brigade, the Muslims' forces were on the hill and we were down. There was not a single metre where our line was up there. We were down there. You can exactly see this by looking at the elevation points along the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long was this line in kilometres, approximately speaking? You don't have to draw the line. Can you just tell us the length?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 20 kilometres approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this map be given a number as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as D211.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to make this even clearer --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell me something more about all this after I've shown you another map? That's 65 ter 2829, if it can be brought up very briefly so that we can talk about this map, in view of what you said before? Mr. Krsman, first, can you see these red and yellow lines on this map?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us on this map and mark the area that was under the control of the group to which you belonged at the time?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map corresponds in the percentage of 90 per cent to the one that I drew except in this area, when our positions were moved like this on the 12th of June. So this entire red line reflects the actual situation as at 12th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're saying. This blue line was there when?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 12th of June 1993, when we were pushed a little bit from that area. [Marks]. This is the only change that took place on the 12th of June and this red line did not change throughout the war. And this change occurred on the day when they pushed us back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now draw the entire line in the area under the control of the group of people to which you belonged?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. So it coincides with the red line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many kilometres is that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a minute ago about 20. I think about 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, to be entirely clear, this little area above the red line and what you encircled now with the blue line, does that mean that the red line, after that date that you mentioned, actually ran along the blue line?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The blue and the red lines were completely identical except in this part when we were attacked on the 12th of June and pushed further back into our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me now something about the people who were issued with the weapons? What happened? What happened next with regard to these things concerning what was being done by the people who were given the weapons on your side? As you mentioned, there were 200 of them. What happened with these men?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set up a defence line in our village. Soon after that the army of Republika Srpska was established. We organised ourselves in a battalion or a brigade, and we did not properly fortify our positions initially but as the war progressed we fortified our positions better, preventing the enemy from pushing us further back into our territory. We were guarding our lives and our houses and the land where we lived for over 300 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you return to your house, your home, after the Dayton?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: My house was burned down in 1992. Not only my house. All the other houses that were on the separation line. And I know the exact figures. Of the 8.700 inhabitants of Rajlovac, there are fewer than 50 of them now, and they are all older than 70 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the line that you have drawn, and after these positions were taken over as you told us, what could you see viewing or if you look at the area where you used to live?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this end point, after the halfway through of the line, is the forested area. Our combatants, myself included, could see from our trenches only the positions of the BH army soldiers and the sky, and nothing else. I'm talking about this forested area because we were down looking upwards towards them. The distance between us was from 30 to 70 metres, and in the suburban area approximately from the Rajlovac barracks to the river Miljacka, the trenches ran along the railway tracks and since we were again down and it was not such a steep slope, we were able to see their trenches and only the first or the second lines of their houses behind these trenches. Absolutely nothing else. Not from a single metre of the line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, you are saying that your house and the houses of your neighbours were burnt down. Can you tell us more specifically in which conditions and context these houses were burnt? Was it because they were on the front line and that therefore they were in a way collateral damage to the warring activities, or were they burnt down in other circumstances? And if so, who burnt them down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 12th of June, that is to say when they attacked our village and when they repelled us further into the territory, about 500 metres away, all the houses were torched. First they were looted and then they were torched with gasoline, matches and so on. So it's not collateral damage. It's not shells. It's not bullets. Most probably gasoline and matches. Things like that. They were razed to the ground. First they were looted and then they were burned and it became their territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much but you haven't told us who burnt them down precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was done by the members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we were at war with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now that we are on the subject, can you tell us, before this war broke out, what was your life like with these people there in that same territory for decades?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never had a single problem whatsoever, interethnic or any other. We visited each other for Christmas, for the Bajram holidays, but this only pertained to the indigenous population living there for hundreds of years, although there were less of them than us. When these people from eastern Bosnia, Serbia, Sandzak, came, these Muslims, all of it changed and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, after you got armed and took up these positions, where did you live when you weren't at the front line?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: 90 per cent of the population of my village moved out, moved away, to stay with relatives, friends, some to Serbia, some to Pale, some to Croatia, some went abroad, whereas we stayed mostly in the area of Vogosca, Rjecica and people who had nowhere to go stayed in the Rajlovac barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark this with a little circle where this Vogosca is and where it was that you lived approximately?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. Vogosca. The Rajlovac barracks. And this territory behind the line, these villages, Rjecica, Dobrosevici, Reljevo. This is where all the refugees from Zabrdje were, hoping that things would calm down and that we would regain those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges now, if you look at this blue line that you finished somewhere below Nisici and then there is this red line going to Nisici, what is the view like from that line and from these places that were under the control of the people who comprised the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, if I can put it that way, and what was the view they had in view of the territories that were within the red line?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: It so happens that I know because I have a lot of relatives. All of us in Sarajevo have lots of relatives in all parts of town. They didn't see anything after this first line here because Zuc, Golo Brdo and Hum are the dominant features there along this line, and this part of town. You cannot see anything in depth in the territory, in town, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you extend the blue line all the way to the place where you think that there is a view, as far as the city is concerned?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]. I know for sure that you cannot see beyond this. I didn't go further up because I had no opportunity to do so. Other people will probably be in a position to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this map please be admitted into evidence in this form as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What you marked in this circle, what is that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vogosca, the Rajlovac barracks and the area from which the population moved or rather the population expelled from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could this circle then include the letter V, please?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The blue line doesn't go to Nisici, further on to the end, where does it go?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the blue line goes to Kobilja Glava and further on to the old city and then further on across to Baric [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this now please be marked once again as yet a new piece of evidence, a new Defence Exhibit, if possible? Not necessarily, Your Honour, it's not indispensable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Doesn't appear to be necessary, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I agree. Yes. It's a misunderstanding with the accused at one point in time about this. That's why I asked. But then I don't think it really matters. It was a slip of the tongue, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic was appointed commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija core?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know approximately that it was somewhere in August or September. To tell you the truth, it's not that we weren't interested in the commanders but they didn't really matter. What mattered was that we carry out our defence tasks, protecting our young and infirm, but I think that it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hold a particular position, if view of the people that you were there with?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was squad leader, platoon leader and finally company leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for me personally, it was Zoran Terzic, Battalion commander. He was also born in our village of Zabrdje. His house is below mine, about 100 metres away, an active duty officer. Captain First Class was the rank he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before he became a commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, I mean General Dragomir Milosevic, at these lines, was anything happening there actually and if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after this fighting in 1993, early in spring 1994, there was an order to withdraw heavy weaponry at ranges over 20 kilometres from town. This was a separation line. We ourselves did not know what this was supposed to mean. That is to say that all weapons with a calibre exceeding 12.7 millimetres, mortars, cannons, all of them had to be moved out from the positions held by our brigade and the entire Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, what I asked you was what was at these lines? Were there any conflicts at these lines?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sporadically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you're not understanding me. First I asked you up until the appointment of General Milosevic, were there any conflicts there? Until when were there intensive conflicts at these lines?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were intensive conflicts throughout 1993, up until the spring of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And when General Dragomir Milosevic assumed his duties, what was the situation like then?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the general assumed his duties, there was a cease-fire signed in August-September, I think, those two months, all the way up until November when this offensive started from all the positions of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In November? When did the conflict start?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflict started in October but in November the fighting was the fiercest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was it that conflicts started in October?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every morning, we had meetings at the command, and during those months we noticed -- or, rather, we received information through our communication systems that the forces of the BH army were withdrawing from town through the well-known tunnel and that they were regrouping at the positions that were behind our back. This is from the Nisic plateau all the way to Kiseljak. And the situation was highly critical, all the way up until that moment when the offensive started.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was the heavy weaponry, then?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a few moments ago, we got everything out, mortars, cannons, everything. We got it all out, 20 kilometres away from us, down the road towards the Nisic plateau, except for a mortar battery that was strictly under the control of UNPROFOR. And one tank, sorry about that. One tank stayed behind. We couldn't get it out because it had been broken. Its hydraulic components were not working. It could not move about at all. So we had lots of trouble getting it out of Rajlovac towards Nisici. We did it together with UNPROFOR and then it stayed up there. I don't know what happened to it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to show you a document, DD003553. You see this document? Please see whose document it is, who issued it on what date and who signed it.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was issued by the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and it was signed by General Milosevic. It says that artillery pieces were moved out of the zone 20 kilometres away, and this tank, I guess that was the tank, stayed behind because it was out of order and it was being moved out towards Cevljanovici and that it will be completed by 1100 hours. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could this please be admitted into evidence as a Defence Exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what the orders looked like, the orders issued to you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orders issued to me throughout the war, as to a superior officer who was supposed to issue these orders to the soldiers on the front line, they were always practically identical, strictly protect your own positions, defend them, strictly defend, defend only, your own positions. Shoot only if attacked. Do not squander ammunition. And if there is an attack, if you are attacked, respond as hard as you can, if your positions are attacked or facilities near those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me an accurate answer now? In the territory held by the BH army, how far could you see that territory?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago that strictly from the positions where the trenches were, we couldn't see anything quite literally, but we had observers with binoculars in depth and they followed the movement of troops and they were watching their mortars, their cannons from where they operated and then in the evening we discussed this and we tried to see what we should do to neutralise them if they presented a threat to our positions but from our positions themselves we couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So how far could you see even with binoculars?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three kilometres at a maximum. And all of that is so nearby that it didn't -- how should I put this? -- constitute a threat. Even from there you couldn't fire a rifle. A rifle would not have sufficient range to those positions. I mean small arms, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were these observation posts if were you in the valley?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: These observation posts were two or three kilometres behind this valley on the slopes of a little hill, behind. These were big binoculars that we had and roughly we could see with them and sometimes you could even see something with the naked eye, where things were, what was going on at their actual front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how far behind you were those observation posts?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two to three kilometres behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did these conflicts that you spoke about, that started in October, how long did they last?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts lasted throughout October and November, and the BH army forces managed to cut this route at Srednje and they had us in encirclement because they reached as far as the road, and then we managed to consolidate our lines and to -- our forces, and to regain those lines, and my area of responsibility up there at the Nisici plateau was Mosevacko Brdo, Jasin [phoen]. This was my sector. And I had a platoon there defending those positions lest they should be able to approach us from our backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you didn't have any heavy weapons, because they had been moved out, what happened? What positions did the BH army have from which it could threaten you at Rajlovac, Iljas?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they could -- they posed a threat from any position, any building. They mostly used mortars when they targeted the area of responsibility of my unit and from Sokolje they fired from their tanks and cannons at Ilidza. It was a little bit further away and they could fire at it directly. And as for Grbavica and all the other parts of the city, they could target it at any time from any position within the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about from Igman?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that because my brother had been wounded, and I had to take him to the Zica Hospital. There was a Browning gun firing at the Ilidza Zica Hospital route and the Rapid Reaction Force targeted my positions from Igman in 1994, they managed actually to hit the trench where I was positioned but fortunately there were no consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I observe that one hour and 30 minutes were allotted for the total examination of this witness. Of that time, you have used one hour and ten minutes, which only leaves 20 minutes for the Prosecution to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we asked for three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I correct myself. I understand it's three hours estimated for the total examination. So you have an hour and a half and you have used an hour and ten minutes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I will speed things up and see if I can maybe be a bit more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me when did those conflicts cease, the ones that we were talking about, the ones in October and November, and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conflicts ended in December when a cease-fire was signed, and we received an order that we should not fire a single bullet under any circumstances at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now show you another document. That's 65 ter 00608. Could you please look at this order? Who issued it? What's the date? And if you can read item 4, and if you can then tell me whether this corresponds to what you just told us about the nature of the orders that you received?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the command of the 1st Iljas Brigade. We at Rajlovac received another one like that. Item 4 reads as follows: Open fire only in case of a surprise attack on units and positions, and in any other situation when it is necessary to open fire, inform the OC of the brigade command. I received this command and I conveyed it to all the soldiers but we knew that they would not comply with it, the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document as a Defence Exhibit too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D214, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, what happened in the months that followed? How long did this cease-fire last?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said before, I knew that they would not comply with it for long. It lasted until June 1995, when the same scenario that we saw in November 1994 was repeated again. They attacked us from all positions, in particular from the area of the Nisici plateau from the outside and also from the inside. They attacked strictly on our positions, on our trenches. This was the fiercest attack in the war. They fired all the weapons that they had and for the first time since the war started, they were firing throughout the night at 1.00, at 2.00. Shells were raining at Trnovo. Everything was on fire. And my line was under threat. And at Nisici plateau, there was an attack. Fortunately, in all this misfortune, the Croat forces did not launch any attacks from Kiseljak area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, now that you told us this, could you please show on this large map just approximately from the blue and red line, what areas were held by the Croat side, by the Croat forces? Could you just look at it and then we will go back.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croat forces held the positions -- they had two brigades, the Ban Jelacic Brigade and the King Kresimir Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any exchanges of fire at any time along those lines? Did any side fire on the other at any time?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since we had indigenous Serb population on one side and the Croat indigenous population on the other, we have lived there for 200 or 400 years, no -- fire was never opened from those positions, and this meant a lot to us because we knew that our backs were secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us what happened in June. I would now like to show you a document, if you could tell me whether that corresponds to what you just told us. It's document D107. It's a Defence Exhibit, D107. Could you please read the letterhead and see what it reads below, what kind of a proposal we are talking about and the first paragraph, and then I would like to ask you yet another question. If you can just read that, please, so that we see the date and what this document is all about.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order from the 1st Corps command dated the 26th of June 1995, so this is when the attacks on our positions were at their fiercest. Then it says here, "In order to tie up the aggressor forces around the city and disperse them offering relief to our forces outside the city, they sent proposals, certain proposals."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at page 2, and do you remember any specific events that are related to this period and these developments?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do. I remember they hit a trench up there on the hill, from shock lay Brdo, from Lemezi. Three soldiers were wounded, Tambur, Mile Cuk, and Dragan Krnjaic. This was a direct hit of a shell on the trench.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at page 2 of this document where we are talking about 112th Mountain Brigade. Is this what you were just telling us about?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says target number 3. They ordered them that they should hit Boro Lemez's house with a multiple rocket launcher and that's what they did. And they injured three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell me, in this whole period and at the time when Dragomir Milosevic was the commander and at the time when the attacks were, the conflicts were really the most intense, how many people were killed in your unit and could you please tell me the approximate number of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: 41 persons were killed in my village, six women, a total of 41 people, and more than 50 people were injured. My aunt was killed, and my brother was seriously injured. As far as Rajlovac is concerned, more than 120 people were killed in the barracks and more than 200 people were wounded. They were like stool pigeons there in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions -- no more questions. Well, this is already in evidence. This is not MFI any more. It's already exhibited. It's already a Defence exhibit. And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. But I wanted to ask the witness this: You just told us about the number of persons who were killed. I'd like to ask you, how did this incident start that resulted in the death of all these people? Tell us how it started and how it progressed, how it came to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the 41 people were killed in Zabrdje, in the village where they were born, all -- all of them, all 41. 20 were shot in the head or in the heart with a bullet round.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Killed by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they were fired on by the people in positions facing us. In other words, BH army troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how did that fight start? That's what I wanted to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I want to find out how that -- how did that particular fight begin? Who started it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I explained to you that on the 5th of May, the first attack was launched. That was the first attack in this territory. And it was started by the Green Berets and later on they became the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When precisely was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly on the 5th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What year are we talking about now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. 5th of May, Boro Bjelice, my next door neighbour, was killed by a shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So the attack that led to the death of these 41 people, that was in 1992, the attack by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's when the first casualty fell, the first person was killed. In the four years of war, my village, which had 600 to 700 people, they were -- 40 people were killed, on their door steps, on various dates, at various times, in those four years of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you to help us by telling us how the incident started that led to these killings of the 40 people over the period of four years, and I'm particularly interested in 1994 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to give you a specific example, Nebojsa Vuletic, he was killed in a trench in 1995. A hand-held rocket launcher was fired at his trench and it was a direct hit during the offensive, and it blew his head off. This is a specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So who was responsible for that? Who fired that rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A soldier of the BH army fired that hand-held rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What month of 1995 was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in June 1995. That was the last offensive. And three soldiers that I told you about a few minutes ago were wounded in a trench just next to this one. Fortunately they were not killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And any other specific incidents that you can remember in 1994, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on my line, there were those two incidents in those years. Most people died in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm interested to ascertain whether your people, the Serbs, responded to any of these attacks, because you're telling us that these were attacks launched by the ABiH. Did the Serbs respond to any of these attacks and was any of the ABiH forces killed in your response?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We responded to each attack that targeted our trenches. I don't know whether anyone was killed. No one can know that. I only know who was killed on our side and that many times we had to risk our own lives in order to pull out the dead bodies of the wounded under such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The 41 civilians who were killed, were they killed in 1992 or throughout the four-year period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that they were not all civilians. The total number was 41. And of the 41, six were women, civilians. And I can tell you about each individual incident. In 1992, for example, 15 were killed; another 15 in 1993; three persons in 1994, et cetera; but I can tell you the circumstances of each and every killing, how they were killed and where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krsman. My name is Mr. Sachdeva and I'm going to ask you a few questions. If you need clarification, please let me know. I actually wanted to start by asking you about your role in the SRK in the -- I understand that you're company was within the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And actually before I get to that, since we have the document on the screen, the last document that Mr. Tapuskovic showed you, I just want you to go back to the point where it speaks about target 3. Do you see that there, at the bottom? You earlier spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I just want to confirm with you that these sleeping quarters, soldiers were sleeping in that house, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was Boro Lemez's house. He lived in it. And they used it as a benchmark and actually they hit the trench, not the house itself. The trench was in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. They hit the trench and soldiers were killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they were only wounded. They were not killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Okay. So let's go back to your role. You were a company commander. When were you made a company commander?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed company commander on the 13th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you have platoons underneath you and if you did, how many platoons did you have? What did you command?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had three platoons in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Roughly how many men or military personnel did you command within those three platoons?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had exactly 157 able-bodied men but we also had on our list some 20 soldiers who were wounded but were receiving medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that you were company commander throughout the conflict, that is through to December 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the commander of that company but also of a company in Rajlovac after the commander of the Rajlovac company was seriously wounded, so I stood in for him. I also discharged duties of the line commander at the Nisici plateau while the fighting was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your battalion, that is the next military unit in the hierarchy above your company, you said that the commander was Commander Terzic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And was he commander as well throughout the conflicts up until December 1995?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We asked specifically for him to become our commander. He came in 1993. He was born in the village of Zabrdje and we trusted him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So when he came in 1993 he remained as commander up until 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what was the name of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Rajlovac Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the battalion, as you said earlier, belonged or was part of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Its commander being Dragan Josipovic; is that correct, from 1993 through to 1995?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I don't know exactly which period but he was a true officer and a man of integrity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You gave evidence earlier today about the meetings, the regular meetings you would have with your battalion commander. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I take it that you met with him every day or every other day? How frequently did you meet with him? How frequently did you have these meetings?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefings were held twice a week, and I saw the commander every day because he lived in Zabrdje. He came to visit his parents. We would have coffee and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the other company commanders would also be in these meetings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you weren't meeting with your commander, I presume that you had regular contact, regular communication, with the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the time. I wondered if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's that time of the day. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, we were talking about communication before the break and I asked you whether you had regular communication with the battalion commander and you replied yes. How was that communication -- how did it manifest? What kind of communication did you have?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a wire telephone line connecting us with the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I take it that whenever there was a need for you to communicate with your battalion commander or other officers within the battalion command, you were able to do that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just as you had good communication with your battalion commander, I take it that the battalion commander also had good communication going up the hierarchy, that is to his brigade commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but I think he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And then moving on from there, the brigade commander would have had effective communication with the personnel in the corps command reaching up to General Milosevic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. I know only up to the level of a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In fact, given your four years with -- as a company commander, it's correct to say that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was an effective functioning corps, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in view of the territory that we had to cover, from, for example, Rajko, Rajlovac to Lukavica, I wouldn't put it like that. The territory of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was so huge that we couldn't visit it all by car in one day and you can only imagine how it was to link up all these things. And I'm very sceptical in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But if you were having effective communication with your battalion commander and the battalion commander was most probably having effective communication with his brigade commander, this would have been mirrored throughout the SRK, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said what he certainly knows about. This is again the area of speculation and assumptions, and I don't think that this would be in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there is some merit in that. I think you can ask another question, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, did you ever meet or see Dragan Milosevic, General Dragan Milosevic, while you were a company commander?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him only once at the Nisic plateau in the course of this offensive but I didn't talk to him on that occasion. We just passed each other and that was the only time that I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you're aware, though, that the general would take trips to the field and meet with his brigade commanders and battalion commanders on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He used to come and visit us but unfortunately, I wasn't present then in Rajlovac. He visited the front line very often. He always told us to be careful, not to shoot at the position without any need, to spare the ammunition and to guard our lives and the territory in which we lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that he visited the front line very often and I take it that that is your front line. How often would he visit the front line?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say precisely but he was known as a general who took good care of his troops, who visited his troops and I believe that he spent more time at the front than in the command headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. And it was important for the general to apprise himself of the military situation on the ground, wasn't it, and that's why he made these trips?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But in addition to the military aspect he was also interested in how we were living, did we have food, what was the situation with our families, whether our families were safe, although the military aspect took precedence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. So he was concerned about the morale within the ranks?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among other things, he boosted our morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And in your view as a military man, this sort of action by a general rendered him an effective commander, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic? I'm not likely to agree with you. He can answer that, if you're going to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only think that an opinion cannot be sought from a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He can speak about that. He was a man in command of soldiers himself. Yes, what is your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would give the answer but first I would like the Prosecutor to explain to me what he meant by "an effective commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'd be happy to. What I'm trying to get at is that the general, in conducting these visits, it was important for him to understand the kind of -- the amount of ammunition that a brigade may have, the needs in terms of military arsenal, firstly with respect to weapons?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: A general has his service in charge of that. He receives information from brigade commanders. But a commander wants to look at certain things himself, and I fully understand why he visited the front lines. That applies to every job and equally it applies to a job of a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. I'm going to move on now to the weaponry that you had in your company. I take it you had mortars within your company?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And how many mortars and what kind of mortars did you have?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had 60-millimetre, 82-millimetre mortars, which we handed over in spring 1994, and after that date we didn't have in the company any mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What about howitzers and anti-aircraft fire, anti-aircraft guns? Did you have them as well?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As a company, we didn't have those. That was at the level of the brigade or even at the level of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You did not have artillery support? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that we had no support. I said that we didn't have these weapons in the company, and that was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So are you saying that you had artillery support?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: In case of the attacks that I mentioned, it was impossible for us to defend ourselves with infantry weapons only, and on a few occasions we asked for mortar and artillery support and we regularly received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that artillery support that you asked for and regularly received was in the form of tanks and howitzers, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, after the spring of 1994, we didn't have absolutely anything at our disposal. Prior to that period, we had a broken tank which served as a gun, and I think we had a battery of B-1 guns. Howitzers were used only as a last resort in the event of an all-out attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you refer to the spring of 1994, I take it you're referring to the Total Exclusion Zone agreement; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, do you know why the Total Exclusion Zone agreement was forthcoming, why it was signed?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, we were not very much involved in politics, although we were badly affected by this agreement, because the balance of the BH infantry and our infantry was ten to one, so we literally only had infantry weapons for our defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you were in Sarajevo for the full time in the conflict, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is there a point which you wish to make?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not having any interpretation from the French into English. Would you start again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Just an intervention -- I would just like to say something about the interpretation, or rather, what is written in the transcript. The witness, line 20, where his answer begins on page 36 of the transcript, the witness said at the end of the sentence, "We were left only with infantry weapons but we honoured this agreement." That's what he said at the end of his sentence. And I suppose we can check that by listening to the audio recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I don't intend to do that. I think we should move on, noting the point that you have made, Ms. Isailovic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I was asking for the reason for the Total Exclusion Zone agreement. You -- as a military person in Sarajevo during the war, you knew about the incident at Markale market on the 5th of February 1994, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question said that as a person in Sarajevo. What part of Sarajevo are we talking about? He wasn't in Sarajevo. Yes, he was in Sarajevo, but the question is not precise. I think it should be said specifically and the Prosecutor should be more specific when asking about his presence in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the point. Where were you stationed, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was living in Rajlovac, in the territory controlled by the army of Republika Srpska. I wasn't living in the city of Sarajevo throughout the war, we were outside the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, taking that into account, Mr. Sachdeva, you may ask your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I persist in the question: Did you hear about the incident at Markale market on the 5th of February 1994?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you heard that in that incident, some 66 civilians were killed and 120 were wounded. Did you hear that too?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know that on the 9th of February 1994, the Total Exclusion Zone agreement came into force, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And that agreement ordered the -- inter alia, in part, ordered the Bosnian Serb army to remove all heavy weapons beyond 20 kilometres from the city. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you gave evidence today that at least with respect to your responsibility in Rajlovac, you honoured that agreement and removed all your heavy weapons beyond 20 kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just as you did that, the other company commanders and the battalion and brigade commanders also complied with that agreement and removed their weapons, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it was important for you to honour this agreement precisely because there was an UNPROFOR -- there was UNPROFOR presence in Rajlovac, wasn't there, from 1993 onwards?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was present in Rajlovac throughout the war, particularly for the reason of the central storehouse for food was located there, and it was in our interests not to fire at UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And one of the main tasks of UNPROFOR --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Isailovic is on her feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. -- could there be -- I want to say something about the transcript. I'm trying to use that facility particularly for the reason of my being able to understand all three languages. On page 39, line 9, the witness's answer is not recorded properly. And I wouldn't like to give an answer instead of him but it reads here: "It was in our interests not to fire at UNPROFOR," and this is not at all what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask the witness, what did you say, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that throughout the war activities, UNPROFOR forces were stationed in Rajlovac, primarily for the reason of the humanitarian aid going from airport to Rajlovac and then distributed into the city from Rajlovac, and this is what they checked, among other things, and they also checked heavy weaponry in that period prior to its withdrawal beyond the 20 kilometre zone. And we never had any problems with UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Witness, in your earlier answer did you say that it was in our interests not to fire at UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did you say in relation to that issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that it was in our interest for UNPROFOR to be there to see who was the one who was shooting first, that we were never the first to shoot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I just want to follow up from your previous answer about UNPROFOR and the heavy weaponry. Is it your evidence that while you were company commander, you never received any complaints from UNPROFOR or protests from UNPROFOR about deviation from the Total Exclusion Zone agreement or any violation of that agreement? Is that what you're telling the Court?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to bring up 65 ter 00066.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I'm just going to show you a document in a moment. Mr. Krsman, while that document is being brought up, you know that 20-millimetre guns that were mounted on vehicles were also excluded in this-- in the TEZ agreement; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the English version. Mr. Krsman, I apologise, sometimes we have some technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the document, Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, you can see on the front, in the B/C/S version, the language -- in your language, that this is a document from the United Nations, from UNPROFOR. It says, "Headquarters BH command forward Sarajevo." Do you see that there at the top?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see that it's dated -- if you look at the bottom of the table, it says subject, and the date is the 10th of December 1994. Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask the Court usher to move to the second page, please -- actually, I apologise, I think it's the third page in the B/C/S version that I'm interested in. Great. Thank you. Mr. Krsman, you see at point 2 there, do you see where it says the subject is titled, "Heavy weapons exclusion zone violations"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I'm just going to read to you what it says there, entitled, "Sarajevo TEZ," which we know to be the Total Exclusion Zone, "At 1011 on the 10th of December 1994, one twin-barrelled 20-millimetre AAA gun mounted on a truck was observed at GRBP 843617. A protest was sent to Rajlovac Battalion, BSA," and BSA is the Bosnian Serb army. Now, upon seeing that report, is it still your evidence that you did not violate the Total Exclusion Zone agreement?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the gentleman who sent this saw, but it says here that what was observed was a gun that was mounted on a trailer truck. So it's not that it was firing, and the protest was not lodged on account of that. Had we wanted to hide it, we wouldn't have displayed it in public this way. This is probably something that looked like a gun or that was being transported in a different direction, not in broad daylight at 11.00, would you place a gun on a truck and it was not operating and you see that here too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, you should let us know about the source of the document, its provenance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understood that I asked a question of the witness whether it was a UN UNPROFOR document and he replied yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I see your answer but it's correct, is it not, that the agreement did not say these weapons should be -- should not be fired. The agreement said these weapons should be removed to beyond 20 kilometres from the city. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that, but I'm saying that if this gun is on a trailer truck, you know how big a trailer truck is, 20 tonnes, and I know with 100 per cent certainty that a 20-millimetre gun was never on that kind of a trailer truck. If they saw it, they probably had withdrawn all the equipment that was decommissioned. They were taking it to the iron works or wherever you're supposed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: On what basis are you saying it's a trailer truck? In the original document it talks about a gun mounted on a truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in B/C/S, the translation concerning this truck, it says trailer truck. So the translation in B/C/S says trailer truck. Now, is the translation good? Because that is a vehicle that only transports things that are supposed to be removed, taken away. It's something for transporting things. It is not a vehicle that can be used in another way. So it is not a truck. It is a trailer truck. It's the biggest possible truck that exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that it is a UN document. Which one is the authoritative one, the UN one or the B/C/S version? So basically, I'm saying where does this document come from? We have two documents here. We have a document in English and a document in B/C/S. Is it that both are not matching, that the translations do not match? Which is the original, the authoritative version. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Mindua, the original is the United Nations document, which is written in English. That would be the authoritative version, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Well, let us examine this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, the United Nations document records that the truck -- the gun was mounted on a truck, and you earlier told the Court that such weapons, if mounted on a vehicle, on a moving vehicle, were prohibited within the TEZ agreement, you said that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the Rajlovac Battalion is your battalion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you receive a protest from the UN at that time? Do you remember now?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
