utterances.text: I do not. Maybe the battalion commander had received it, but I, as company commander, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you hear of your battalion commander receiving such a protest?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear of it because we observed the cease-fire then in December all the way up to June 1995, practically not a single bullet was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So in spite of this document, your evidence remains the same, that you did not violate the TEZ agreement or that your battalion did not violate the TEZ agreement?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: We certainly did not fire. I am telling you that this is probably a gun that was out of order, and that was put on this trailer truck and that was being taken away for decommissioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P760, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know why the B/C/S would translate "truck" as "trailer truck."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Perhaps the Prosecution can arrange for another translation, although the exhibit is in its original form. That is in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't ask for that. I don't consider it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I moved on to the Total Exclusion Zone because you started talking about your mortars so I want to move back to talk more about weapons, not necessarily within your company but also within your battalion and brigade. In the period 1994 through to 1995, you must have known about modified air bombs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in our company or battalion and even in brigade, I believe, did I see any such thing or did I hear of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you know what a modified air bomb is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what an air bomb is, and I know that from television. I actually never saw it in real life. As for a modified air bomb, I don't know. I really do not know. Because we had all sorts of weapons, but that I had never seen, ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. If you just listen to my question carefully, I'm not asking you whether you saw one. You know what an air bomb is and those bombs are dropped from air planes, aren't they? They are designed to be dropped from airplanes?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, he's already responded, and now, "Do you know?" If he said that he had never seen it and doesn't know what it is, how can he be asked yet again? He's already given an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But counsel is probing. He's going a little further. He says you know what an air bomb is and those bombs are dropped from airplanes, aren't they? So he's moving on. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sir, you've just told the Court that you know that these bombs are originally designed to be dropped from airplanes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you are aware, I suggest, that during the period 1994, 1995, the Bosnian Serb army, and in particular your brigade, modified these air bombs and fired them from within its area of responsibility. You're aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely not correct. I certainly would have known about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you're telling the Court that if indeed your brigade, that is the 3rd Infantry Brigade, had these air bombs, these modified air bombs, you as a company commander would have known about it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least I would have heard of it having been fired but I absolutely never saw any such thing, especially not in the area of responsibility of my battalion or do we need it or do I know what it's used for or what kind of objectives it can target.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You know that these modified air bombs are inaccurate weapons; don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I didn't even know what they looked like, but if they are modified, then most probably they are inaccurate. But I really don't even know what they look like and how they are fired or launched or thrown, whatever. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You never heard that they were modified by the attachment of rockets to the bomb and then fired from a truck? You didn't hear that in your time as a company commander in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. This is the first time I hear of it in my life. Not that I've seen it ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Presumably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is the first time you're hearing of a modified air bomb? Is that your testimony, that you're hearing for the first time in this courtroom of the use of a modified air bomb? That's an air bomb with rockets attached to it, fired from a truck. Are you saying that this is the first time you're hearing of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said that this is the first time I hear of rockets being placed on them and this is the first time I hear that they have been used in Rajlovac in the area of responsibility of my battalion. That is what I hear for the first time. I have heard of the expression modified air bomb. I've heard the expression. But I never saw this and we never used this in the war in my battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But they were used by your brigade, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. My battalion certainly didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In fact, these modified air bombs were fired from Butile which is within the area of responsibility of the VRS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is that area of responsibility but I'm not aware of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You know that the TV tower in Sarajevo was hit by a modified air bomb, don't you? You must have heard about that.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that on television when the TV tower was hit but I don't know with what weapon. It is quite impossible to determine with what weapon it was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to call up 65 ter 03191.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, you see a document there on the right-hand side of the screen. You see at the top it says, "Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that it is an authentic document from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, would you not?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if we just scroll down to the end or actually in the B/C/S version, you can see that it was signed by the Chief of Staff, Cedomir Sladoje? You see that there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm just giving you a few minutes to read the text but in the interest of time, it's clear that this document is ordering the supply of five pieces, five modified air bombs, three 105-kilograms and two 250-kilograms to the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, which is your brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I beg your pardon. May I? Since I absolutely perfectly know my own language, I can say it says "very urgent," it just says "very urgent, submit to." There is no order, no order whatsoever. And the witness heard it being said, "Order" that this is some kind of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we take that into account, but Mr. Sachdeva, I don't myself see any reference to the term modified air bomb in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, there has been evidence in this trial that the -- what the Prosecution has alleged, that is modified air bombs being used on Sarajevo were termed, were given this term, FAB, aerial bomb. In our submission, this refers to modified air bombs. This is what we have seen in other documents that have been admitted in this trial. I don't -- I'm not sure if this is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But how can you put that to the witness in that way? Because the witness would not know what the evidence has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to the witness that the -- what's indicated here, the FAB 105 KG and the FAB 250 KG are in fact modified air bombs to be delivered to his brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. What do you say to that, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I stand by what I said, and secondly, FAB 250 kilograms and 105 kilograms is first of all an air bomb. It doesn't say modified air bomb anywhere in this text. It is an air bomb. What is mentioned here, that is, that is an air bomb. And it would have to say, if it's modified, that it is a modified air bomb. It would have to say so in the text but there is no reference whatsoever to a modified air bomb, so that is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, I won't allow the question to be put in the way that you formulated it because it misrepresents the document because there is no reference in the document to modified air bomb, so you might wish to reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And could I add to the President's question that it appears to be somewhat unclear who these bombs, modified or not, are to be delivered to. My reading of the text in front of us is that these bombs are to be delivered to the 1st Brigade and not to the 3rd. And so that the commander of the 3rd Brigade is to be informed of the delivery of these bombs to the 1st Brigade and if I have understood it correctly, the witness is or was the commander of a company under the 3rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, my understanding is, with respect, different. In other words, the order is to be -- or excuse me, I won't characterise it as an order but the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It does say it's an order to be -- at least in the English version, it says, "To be delivered to the 1st Brigade" and then in parentheses, "as an order."

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my submission, the part that says "to be delivered to" is in respect of the document, and the document is therefore for information to the commander of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, because underneath that initial line it says, "Pursuant to the decision of the SRK commander, you are to hand over immediately the following materials to the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade" and then, in my submission, it lists the materials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't see that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I'll persist with the question but I will reformulate it. You can see here that this is a document requesting that three pieces of FAB 105 KG air bomb and two pieces of FAB 250 KG air bomb are to be delivered immediately to the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade. You see that there, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see here under item 1, FAB 105 kilograms, three pieces and item number 2 is FAB 250 kilograms, two pieces. If you hadn't told me now, I wouldn't have known that this actually refers to bombs, to air bombs. I would not have known that if you had not told me that. This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, then: It's correct that you know, then, that the 3rd Infantry Brigade had these FAB bombs in its arsenal? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, and I categorically claim that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I did not intervene a moment ago, but my learned colleague from the Prosecution uses terms, "you have to," "it is demanded." But it doesn't say in this document here, and this is again a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's just reflecting the English, that "you are to hand over immediately the following materials, material supplies." It doesn't say that in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, this would be a debatable linguistic nature. I don't want to raise those issues. It is very strict in our language. But I don't want to go into any debate on that but I don't think that we should really replace words with other words. If they say immediately, then it means one thing. But -- and I'm fine with that. But please, we should not have other words added which are not there, such as, "You must" or "I order," because they are not there in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I follow the point but "you are to hand over immediately" looks to me very much like an order. Proceed, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, in your brigade or in your battalion or in your company even, how many air bombers did you have? How many bomber planes did you have?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the translation is correct but we had one bomber aircraft.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apologies. We didn't hear --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I heard in interpretation is "bomb, bomber aircraft." We did not have any aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can I just -- let me just confirm that your evidence is that you did not have any bomber aircraft; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, how can a company have a bomber aircraft?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But also your brigade did not have them either, did they?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's absolutely true, what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And so, if these FAB bombs are air bombs, there was no plan to use them from planes, was there? There was no plan to drop them from planes?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P761, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krsman, you in your evidence-in-chief, you talked about observers. Do you remember talking about that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And I think you said that your company or let's say your battalion had observers that could -- well, that you had observers in the field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you know with respect to mortars, the use of observers is typical in picking out targets, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't really use those observers for any purpose. I can't see the point of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you had observers in the field that would radio back to those personnel manning the weapons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody notified any of our crews about anything, of the observers. Do you mean the UN observers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the evidence you gave earlier about -- you said that you had observers in the field that would provide information about the whereabouts of the enemy. Do you remember saying that? I'm paraphrasing what you said but I think that's along the lines of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the term that we use in B/C/S means that they merely observe things. Yes, we did have observers in that sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when they observed things and they received or they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Sachdeva, but Ms. Isailovic has a point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, there is a difference in B/C/S and I was trying to find the word in French and in fact it's reconnaissance mainly rather than observer and I'm not sure what they said in English, but I'm not sure of the word in English. I don't really know. I don't speak English, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Isailovic. Mr. Sachdeva?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, when they perform their duty in observing the locations of the enemy, they would -- that information would be relayed to the command, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just as your company or your battalion had these observers, you would agree with me that other brigades and other battalions within the SRK employed this use of observers to locate targets?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for my battalion I often personally went to observe the line. As for the other battalions, I don't know. They may have those or not. I can't tell you something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you also talked -- well, I asked you in the beginning about the platoons and you said you had three platoons within your company that you commanded. You remember telling me that, or telling the Court that, sorry?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And each platoon would comprise how many men?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each platoon had between 50 and 60 people. It would depend on the casualties. If somebody got wounded, then they would leave the platoon, but in general, 50 to 60 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And within the platoon, you had -- you had persons that were snipers or sharp shooters, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my company, and in fact in no company that was in the Rajlovac Brigade, did we have a single sniper, because we couldn't even use those.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But within your brigade there were snipers, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any snipers. As far as I know, snipers have to undergo special training. They have their very strict tasks. And in our brigade, I can say that with certainty, in our battalion, we didn't have a single sniper. I don't know about the brigade but I do have my doubts. But you have to ask somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to talk to you about that, the training in a moment but let's move away from the term snipers. You had within the company and within the Battalion, you had infantry men with rifles and machine-guns, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of our battalion had light weapons, rifles, and the machine-guns were located at certain points and they were not carried here and there on the line. They were not moved along the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is it your evidence that your company and other companies never employed the use of snipers or persons that were trained within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for us to do so and we didn't have snipers because I already explained in my examination-in-chief, our positions were in the valley and we definitely could not use snipers at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to call up 65 ter 02197.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krsman, you see that this is a document, a report on order from the command of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, do you see that, dated 15th January 1995?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you already told the Court that the commander was -- at least at this stage was Dragan Josipovic. Do you remember telling that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I could ask the Court usher to move to the last page on both versions, please. You see at the bottom there, the stamp and the name Dragan Josipovic, Lieutenant-Colonel Dragan Josipovic. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: This is a valid authentic document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if I could ask to move to the penultimate page, that's the one just before this one, do you see just above a list, you see where it says, "We would recommend the following for training as snipers" and it lists some names, Miroslavka Ivetic, Slavko Peric, Aleksandar Jokic, Zoran Sucur? You see that there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you agree with me that this is a document signed by the commander of the 3rd Infantry Brigade recommending persons within his command for sniper training? You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document lists a number of tasks that have to be carried out by the instructors, and one of these tasks is to train the snipers, although I don't know any of those four people. There is even a female name, Miroslavka Ivetic. That's a female name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So you would agree that the third infantry brigade had snipers, trained people for -- well, you would agree that they trained people to perform sniping duties, amongst other things?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that there are plans for them to undergo training. I don't know if they really underwent training or not because you cannot see this from this document. That's one thing. And most probably there are snipers in the military, in accordance with the establishment, the structure. All I know that we didn't have any in our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to understand your answer. Are you still maintaining your evidence that there were no snipers within the 3rd Infantry Brigade? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said, and what I still maintain, is that there were no snipers in my battalion and there were no people who fired from sniper rifles. As for the brigade, I don't know. I can see now this information but I don't know whether they actually underwent this training because a number of orders would be issued and then they were not complied with or they were not carried out because fighting would break out so I don't know in this particular case whether this was actually effected.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P762, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I want to move on to another document and I see the time and I'm wondering whether it's an appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe the break is at -- I believe it's at 25 minutes to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may I have a point of clarification for the record. The previous document 65 ter number 02197 that we admitted as P762 was already in evidence as P682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court deputy will attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I want to bring up a document that I have informed the Defence of which was not on my initial list. I have informed the Defence and I understand they have no objections, and so I'm seeking your leave to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If I could ask for -- thank you, Mr. President. If I could ask for 65 ter 03208 to be brought up, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Witness, you see a document there on your screen? You see that there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you see it's to the Sarajevo -- it's from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command and it's also noted there that the Main Staff of the VRS is informed. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it appears to have been drafted by Colonel Bosko Pasic, the assistant commander for logistics, as of 25th of June 1992. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you can see that the text states that, "Based on a conversation with General Mladic, the commander of the army of the SR BiH, we hereby ask to you provide the following equipment for the needs of the Rajlovac Brigade." And it lists 50 camouflage uniforms, eight snipers, and 20 pistols. You see that there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And at that time, the Rajlovac Brigade was your brigade, wasn't it? You were a member of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So I suggest to you, Mr. Krsman, that you did indeed have snipers. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: We absolutely didn't have any snipers. I can state that with full responsibility, moral, whatever you want. My battalion and in particular my company never had any snipers on the line, and I don't know this Colonel Bosko Pasic. I know General Mladic, although I have never seen him. This is at the beginning of the war and they are asking for something to be provided. Now, as to whether this really was provided and to whom, I don't know. As for pistols, I did not see -- I may have seen two pistols during the entire war and they were in the property of officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So in spite of this document and the previous document, that is your evidence: There were no snipers in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me state again: In my battalion I'm sure there weren't any. I don't know about the brigade because I didn't control the brigade. I knew what the situation was in my battalion and in particular in my company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P763, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only ask you to keep an eye on the time allotted to the Prosecutor, because we have to respect those time limits. I know how it was when the -- during the Prosecution case. It's not just us who are bound by those deadlines. It's the Prosecution too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of course I intend to do exactly that. Mr. Sachdeva had an hour and 30 minutes, and so far he has used about an hour and 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, I just want to ask you about the AOR of your brigade, the 3rd Infantry Brigade. It's correct, isn't it, that -- it ranges from the Rajlovac area towards in the west -- from the west northwest, towards Mirkovici and included the Kosver [phoen] Brigade in Mirkovici; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And it also included a feature known as Spicasta Stijena, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about it but I never actually went to those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: But you know that Spicasta Stijena is a ridge and below it is a place called Gordonja [phoen], you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I have never been there in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Well, you answered that you heard about it so you heard that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps controlled Spicasta Stijena; you heard that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And although you haven't been there, you know that the location of Spicasta Stijena permitted commanding views over the city, and in particular, the village of Sedrenik; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. If I knew, I would tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you heard -- you also heard that the SRK soldiers on Spicasta Stijena would snipe or fire shots into the village of Sedrenik and hit civilians, you heard that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that on the news. That was Muslim propaganda. I never heard any such reports from our officers or from our soldiers. I really don't know where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You used to watch the news on a regular basis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I had free time, I did watch the news. And also whenever there was electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And presumably your colleagues and other persons in the military would also watch the news?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends. Sometimes they did, sometimes they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So it's fair to say that you and your colleagues must have known about what was happening in Sarajevo and that civilians were being killed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was war, and everyone was exposed to fire, both their population and our population, their fighters and our fighters, people get killed in a war, and I really don't know who was killed, how many people were killed. All I know is about our side. According to the reports on the Muslim television, if you would add up all the figures that they stated about those who were killed in their news bulletins, the whole population of Bosnia-Herzegovina wouldn't be sufficient according to how many they claim were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about figures. I'm simply asking you to tell the Court that you heard or you saw on the news that civilians were being killed and wounded inside the city of Sarajevo. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: We followed both news bulletins, just as they showed their civilians being killed, we also saw our children being killed in Grbavica, in Mirkovici, in Ilidza, in Rajlovac, and I suppose that was also the case in Sarajevo. I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: It was the case in Sarajevo because the SRK, your colleagues in the military, were firing their weapons into the city. They were shelling the city, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: My company, my platoon, my battalion, never fired at civilians. We exclusively fired at military positions of members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the positions from which different weapons were fired from, regardless of where they were positioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So whenever you were -- I take it from your answer that if the enemy was firing at you, you would return fire, irrespective of where that position was; is that right? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a gun fired, for instance, for a position identified by our observer, we would target this location from which the gun had fired. I'm telling you very precisely. In the area of responsibility of my battalion, there were no civilians at -- where we could see not at two or three kilometres. What we could see were only the -- see their trenches, so it was absolutely impossible for to us target civilians because they weren't there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Wasn't there a mosque in your area? At least there was a mosque that you could see, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It's still there, at Sokolj on the hill above us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, how much more time will you be needing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think ten more minutes. I know I've said that before, but I do believe ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, just a final issue. When I asked you before the break -- my question was: "So wherever you were, I take it from your answer, if the enemy was firing at you, you would return fire, irrespective of where that position was; is that right? Is that what you're saying?" And your answer was: "If a gun fired, for instance, for a position" -- but I suspect -- "for a position identified by our observer, we would target this location from which the gun had fired." Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And this course of action was employed throughout the war, and in 1994 and 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1994 and 1995, we didn't have heavy weapons to target these positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How would you respond? What weapons would you use?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would call the battalion command, the battalion command would call the brigade command, and then the weapons under the brigade command would target -- or engage this target.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What kind of weapons?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on what weapons were used at their position. If it was a gun, we would respond with a gun. If it was a mortar, we would try to locate it and we would respond with either a gun or a mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What kind of mortars would you respond with?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since at their positions they had a mortar mounted on a vehicle, and it frequently changed place, we would identify its location and wait for it to appear to fire shells. Then we would fire at it from a B-1 gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said you also used mortars, you would fire at these positions with -- you said in your company you had 82-millimetre mortars and 60-millimetre mortars; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up until 1984 [as interpreted], until the order of withdrawal came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You mean 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sachdeva. Any re-examination, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I have a small question to the witness relating to your testimony about Spicasta Stijena and I understood you to say that this was held by the SRK; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know if the SRK had trenches on Spicasta Stijena?

utterances.speaker: Sinisa Krsman [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that we were holding these positions and the line but I don't know precisely because I personally never went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Krsman, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to testify. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And your next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Mr. Vaso Elez. T17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit, and you may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And by means of introductory questions, I'm going to directly examine the witness in order to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell the Judges your full name?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: My name is Vaso Elez.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to tell you in advance, and I already explained this to you, but just please be careful not to answer before the cursor in front of you on the screen has stopped, and I on my part will also pay attention to that. Through this examination, then, I will finalise it more easily. You were born on the 30th of June 1959?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born in Poljice, Foca municipality, in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have been living in Sarajevo since 1969?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You finished elementary school in the school which was situated in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The secondary school for wood processing, you completed in Pofalici in Sarajevo in 1979?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your profession, for which you were educated, you were employed in Sipat from 1980 until 1982?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Like any other citizen of the then state, you fulfilled your civil duty and served one year in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1982?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your return from the Yugoslav People's Army in 1983, you found a job again in Sipat Company and you remained in Sipat until 1992 in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like now to show you a map, a city map, because I think that would be the best way for you to explain certain things to us. It's document D22. Something has already been marked on this map, whereas I required a blank map. That's 65 ter 2872. My mistake. I apologise. Can the southern part be zoomed in or can we scroll the map a bit? To the right a little bit more, please, and if it can be enlarged? Now it's all right. Can we please enlarge a little? I think this is going to be all right. Mr. Vaso, can you show us on the map where your family house was and where you used to live? Can you do that on this map? It has to be moved to the right a little bit more. Is it all right now?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: This map is rather small for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Shall we try and enlarge it as it is now?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it better now?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: This will be good enough for me to find my way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where your family house is?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: My family house is here. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please put a letter K next to it, next to this circle?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You lived there with whom?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: I lived in my family house with my mother, my brother and his family, until 1983, when I moved to Grbavica to a flat on 107 Lenjinova Street. I moved there with my wife and her mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where that was, the street and the building that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes, I can. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please put a letter L?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when conflicts broke out, what happened with those people who were living in your family house?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: When the conflicts broke out, in Grbavica, my brother and his family left. My mother remained alone. I continued living in the flat at Grbavica, and I was observing the events or following the developments in Bosnia on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please say what it was that happened to your brother? Where did he go?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: My brother went to Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ever return again after those events? Just give me a brief answer.

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: He did not return.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who was there from your family at the moment when the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: My wife, my seven-year-old daughter, my mother-in-law, and my own mother, in our family home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict, as for this building where you lived with them, did they go anywhere from there?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: During the conflicts that went on for four years, my family did not go anywhere. They were there with me at Grbavica and Kovacici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges what happened during those days and months in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: As for the very beginning of 1992, I was not a participant. I was an observer, by way of the media. That is to say that when the unrest started, when the shooting started, it was impossible to go to work, the streets became empty. Fear prevailed, which was my case, too. I was afraid. I was wondering what to do. After what happened happened in the barracks in Sarajevo, after the attack on the troops in Dobrovoljacka Street in May, in Pofalici, the people who went over to Grbavica were saying that there were a lot of killings, many people were captured, many people went missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How and when did you take a weapon or receive a weapon, and how did you decide to do that? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Many people were already armed, neighbours, friends. It was not safe to live there when you're afraid for your family and for yourself. That is why I reported and was issued with a so-called Thompson rifle. Others had semi-automatic rifles, automatic rifles. Later on I got an automatic rifle because this Thompson was not safe and there wasn't any ammunition for it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain to the Judges what it meant in peacetime when somebody would say somewhere in a town, "Territorial Defence"?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Territorial Defence; every local commune where people were supposed to prevent -- defend themselves from attacks against the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In order for the Judges to understand this better, when you say, "Attacks against the country," attacks from who?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: The external enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did you live there with your neighbours over all those years where your family home was and where you lived with your family in Sarajevo and Grbavica? What kind of relations did you have?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Relations with the Muslims were friendly, as among friends, neighbours, best friends, relatives. I never believed that what happened during those following four years would happen, namely that they would shoot at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you received these weapons, what happened then? Where was it that you got these weapons exactly? Can you first tell me that? Where and when? At what point in time did this occur?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: I was issued with a weapon in mid-May, at the Territorial Defence Staff at Grbavica, in the Grbavica local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what happened then? You got these weapons and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: I was deployed in a unit which was a company, along the Miljacka river from the Vrbanja bridge to the Bratstva-Jedinstvo Bridge. The area of responsibility of this company was, as I said just now, between the two bridges down the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to indicate that later. I just wanted to ask you what it was that you joined and how all of this developed. Who was it that you joined?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: I joined the army of Republika Srpska in order to defend my life, the life of my family, the property I had at Grbavica, and Kovacici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you given some particular duty then at the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Until the end of 1992, I was an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now indicate what it was like while were you there as a soldier? Can you indicate the separation line between you and if there was someone on the other side? Well, actually, could you say that first? Was there a separation line there between some armies?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: The separation line was by the left bank of the Miljacka. On our side was the army of Republika Srpska. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this carefully. Where are you drawing this? I don't want to lead you. I mean, have you made a mistake or are you doing this right?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Obviously I've made a mistake, a big mistake. I went to the road on the other side. [Marks]. So from the Vrbanja bridge down the Miljacka to the Bratstva-Jedinstvo Bridge. On the other side was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were fortified here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, could you stop there for a moment? Could you just draw the entire separation line, as you had put it, between you and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the area of Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Then from the Vrbanja bridge, part of Beogradska, Ljubljanska, Miska Jovanovica, towards the Jewish cemetery, up to the foot of Debelo Brdo. On Debelo Brdo, there were troops of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Elez, please draw the separation line first and then we are going to discuss other matters. I haven't asked you about any of that yet.

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]. Then along the Miljacka to Streljevac [phoen] towards the Zeljeznicar stadium. And then Sanac, Zagorska, Milinklatska, Ozrenska, those are the streets, towards Djukica Potok and Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this other side, how far did that go?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: You mean what I haven't finished yet, towards Debelo Brdo? It went to Debelo Brdo. If I can find my way on this map, it's roughly around here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark Debelo Brdo now?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And on this side, the other side, the left side, was there a hill over there?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Mojmilo was on the left side. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe what things were like during those first days of the conflict, what life was like in Grbavica, in view of what it was that had started happening, as you had put it?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Life at Grbavica was very hard, both for soldiers and the rest of the population. We were in a low area that could be seen from all sides. On the right-hand was Debelo Brdo which was a lot higher up, and that's where enemy fire was coming from. And also, from the Mojmilo hill, from Samac too, Hrasno. Also from the other side of the Miljacka from taller residential buildings, Grbavica was under gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you first mark this area that you circled just now and you said it was Mojmilo, so could you mark that with the letter M?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the right side, could you place the letter D where you said that Debelo Brdo was?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to save this map as it is marked now, as a -- and to have it tendered as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to go through this introductory part, I have to show the witness a photograph, that's 65 ter photograph 02906. The Prosecutor agreed that I may use this photograph although it was not on our list, but I seek leave from you to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have it enlarged a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Elez, could you please show the house where you lived together with your wife and child?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: You cannot see the house here. You have to move the photograph to the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, the apartment where you lived with your wife and child. What building was this apartment in?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Now I understand. It is this first pavilion type building here. [Marks]. I will mark it here. That is the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what floor were you on?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: On the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark that with a K?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would like to ask you to draw in the separation line between the two warring factions on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: The separation line went along the Miljacka. [Marks]. Only the left and the right-hand side are missing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness said the separation line was the Miljacka river but he hasn't marked the Miljacka river and -- I mean, I don't think this is even a controversial point in this trial anymore. I think that the Prosecution would be perfectly willing to stipulate that the line of separation was the Miljacka river.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can actually see some -- is that water behind it, behind the line? But this is not an exercise in cartography. So there you have it. We know what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like the witness, now that he's drawn in this line, to mark with a different colour pen the position where he was on the separation line during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]. I am now showing you the positions where I was with my platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm asking you. And could you please explain?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: This line that I marked in blue, this is where -- actually it is said that the separation line was the Miljacka river but our positions were at the Pionirski Dom which was abandoned, and also another building, which was a little bit closer to Miljacka, and the school. In 1993, I became a platoon commander, and what I just showed you, that would be the area of responsibility of that platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far was this line from the building where your wife and child lived? How many metres?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: From the building where my family lived to the first positions along the line, it was about 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it like that throughout the war, that your wife and child were actually behind your back?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: My family lived throughout the war in this building, as did the other families, the families that had lived there before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you now draw in approximately where the Bosnia-Herzegovina army forces were stationed?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: The Bosnia-Herzegovina army troops were behind the line of trees, in buildings. In fact, the school of economics, the wood processing school, the faculty of mechanical engineering, Unioninvest company building, the museum. And I don't know what buildings are there further down there. [Marks]. They were fortified, as were we on this side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was it like when clashes broke out?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Well, there would be exchanges of fire, both sides were firing. We would fire on their military targets, their positions, and they would open fire on us. We couldn't really see them because of the trees and other structures there. But on the other side, there were no -- these are not apartment buildings. These were schools, faculty buildings, companies, then in the depths, there is the Marshal Tito barracks where they were actually stationed. Then there is also the railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please -- just a moment. Could you please mark the Marshal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: The Marshal Tito barracks has been torn down. [Marks]. And this was it, what I just marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Those two buildings to the left, to the left of your positions, the two tall buildings, did they have any names?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Do I have to mark them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]. This building was called sibicara, matchbox, because it looked like a matchbox. This is the Energoinvest building. And this here is the faculty of natural sciences and mathematics.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'm going to ask you to mark some things but I wanted to ask you something while I have time. Until what time were you the platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: I was the platoon commander until 1993, until the end of --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain to the Chamber what happened? Why did you cease being a platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: I no longer wanted to be the platoon commander because I could no longer pick and choose the soldiers who would go to Ozrenska to assist their fellow fighters, because every second soldier would get killed and they never came back. I couldn't bear that any longer, and it was easier for me to be just an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the Ozrenska street in relation to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: Ozrenska Street is to the left of Grbavica. It's underneath Mojmilo Brdo. There were some private homes there and the positions were established in those homes, in the houses. Sometimes the distance would be five, six, ten metres, and the BH army soldiers would often break through our lines there, killing people and then they would retreat. This is also what happened on the other flank, the Zagrebacka, Beogradska, Vrbanja bridge, Miska Jovanovica street, Ljubljanska street, where there were those constant raids.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell me how many soldiers got killed by the time when you decided to forgo this position?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: One out of two soldiers were killed, just to give you an example, in this battalion, 150 -- 190 soldiers were killed and out of this number, 120 were killed at Ozrenska street.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please mark this large area where you've just told us what it actually was, could you mark it with the letter T?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The school of mechanical engineering that you marked with M?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The faculty of natural sciences and maths. And could you mark the sibicara building, the matchbox building, with a letter S?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And the last building there, could you mark it with letter C?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the few remaining minutes, could you explain to the Judges -- well, you said that you went back and that you were just an ordinary soldier. That's what you told us. How much time did you spend in the trenches?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: At the part of the front line where my platoon was, at the bank of the River Miljacka, we didn't spend all the time there because we had to go and assist in Sanac, Moravska street, Ozrenska street, and also to the right we had to assist in the area of Vrbanja, Miska Jovanovica street. We couldn't move all that much because the BH army would attack a flank, the -- all of Grbavica would be fire-swept area for rifle fire, for mortar fire, and it was impossible to move at those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me what kind of weapons did the people in your battalion have?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: The soldiers in my platoon had infantry weapons, semi-automatic rifles, automatic rifles. There was an old M-53 machine-gun that didn't really work all the time. It would jam after firing a couple of bullets. It was old Yugoslav weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what other weapons were there at Grbavica? Could you please tell the Judges?

utterances.speaker: VASO ELEZ
utterances.text: There were just infantry weapons at Grbavica. We didn't have other weapons. And we couldn't defend ourselves using any other weapons. The only thing that existed, there was an armoured personnel carrier that was stationed in front of the police building. It was there, ready to evacuate the wounded or the -- those who had been killed. This happened most often at the approach to Belgradeska street which was an area without cover. And it was used to evacuate the dead and the wounded and the same thing went for the other flank. I didn't see any other weapons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my time is now up for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time to adjourn. We'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon in Courtroom I.
